archetype.name: Rebuilding (outshot, young blueline)
archetype.definition: A last-place team from a year ago that still can't control play, leaning on a young back end and a split goaltending tandem while it figures out who belongs in the next good Vancouver team.

report.headline: Hot shooting is hiding the problem: Vancouver can't get or deny the puck
report.take:
Vancouver opened 2026-27 where 2025-26 left it: at the bottom. The site has them 32nd of 32, just as it did last year, when they finished 25-49-8 with 58 points. At 2-7-1 they're on pace for 41 points. This isn't an unlucky good team. Their 5-on-5 xGF % of 39.4% ranks 31st, CF % is 29th, and they're last in the league at 21.1 shots on goal a game while giving up 32.7, 31st.

The overall PDO looks ordinary, 100.8 in all situations, 15th, and that's the trap. Two extremes are canceling out. The skaters are shooting 14.2%, fifth in the league, against a league average of 11.3%. The goalies have stopped .865 of shots, 29th. Goals scored per game sits a respectable 17th only because a tiny shot volume is going in at an unsustainable rate. Paul Cotter has four goals on nine shots, and Linus Karlsson and Marco Rossi have been opportunistic too. Goals allowed sits 31st because that shot flood met a goalie having a disastrous start.

The goaltending split is the most important thing on this sheet. Kevin Lankinen has started six games with a .807 save % and -11 GSAx, last of 65 on the goalie tab. Leevi Merilainen has started four at .925 and +2.8, 15th of 65. The team's -6.7 Goalies GSAx is entirely Lankinen's doing. The penalty kill, at 58.1% and dead last, a full 20-plus points under the league's 79%, compounds it. Up front, Elias Pettersson at center (10 points, 23rd of 220) is the only forward driving anything, and Brock Boeser's 36.1% xGF is a warning sign for a top-six winger. On the blue line, Filip Hronek logs over 25 minutes on a 38.7% xGF. Zeev Buium's 21 minutes a night grade 232nd of 242, which reads like development time rather than a winning choice.

Where is this going? The shooting will cool, and that will cost goals. If Merilainen takes the net, the save percentage should climb by more than enough to offset it. The underlying shot share, though, is a bottom-two team's. The last five games, an 0-4-1 eastern road trip with only 1.8 goals a game, show what the offense looks like when the bounces stop. This is a rebuild year, and the useful question is development, not the standings.

strengths.title: Merilainen has been a real goalie
strengths.body: In four starts Leevi Merilainen has a .925 save % and +2.8 GSAx, ranking 15th of 65 goalies. That's the opposite of his partner, and it shows the goals-against problem is partly a choice of starter. The sample is tiny, but the gap is too large to ignore, and riding him is the fastest fix available.

strengths.title: Pettersson still produces at center
strengths.body: Elias Pettersson has 10 points and five power-play points in 10 games, 23rd of 220 centers. He's the main reason the power play (20%) runs roughly at league average while everything else sinks. His 45% xGF says he's being buried with the rest, but the production at the top is real.

strengths.title: A bright spot on defense
strengths.body: The defenseman Elias Pettersson ranks 13th of 242 on the defense tab, with three goals, a +3 and the best xGF of the regular blueliners at 45.8%. In under 19 minutes a night he's outperforming the players ahead of him in ice time. He looks like a cornerstone of whatever comes next.

concerns.title: Outshot and out-chanced every night
concerns.body: Vancouver gets the fewest shots in the league and allows the second-most, and its expected-goals share is 31st. That's not a goalie or luck problem. It's the forwards and defense losing possession, and it echoes last season's 44.2% xGF. Every defender in the regular rotation sits below 46% xGF, and three of the top five sit below 40%.

concerns.title: Shooting luck propping up offense
concerns.body: A 14.2% shooting rate, fifth in the league and well above the 11.3% norm, is carrying a middling offense on the league's lowest shot volume. That's the part of the record most likely to regress. The last five games, at 1.8 goals a game, already show it cooling.

concerns.title: Lankinen and the penalty kill
concerns.body: Kevin Lankinen's .807 save % and -11 GSAx in six starts are the worst on the goalie tab. The 58.1% penalty kill is last by a wide margin. Both should improve from here because neither is that bad over a full season, but together they explain why goals against ranks 31st.

trend.note: An overtime win at Edmonton and a win over Calgary gave way to a seven-game losing streak. The eastern trip finished 0-4-1 with the offense down to 1.8 goals a game, though the defense was slightly less leaky than its season rate.

weekAhead.headline: Home from the road, straight into two top-five teams
weekAhead.body:
The road trip ends with a homestand that starts brutally. Carolina is first on the site, with A+ grades at forward and on defense, 33.1 shots a game and a 58.6% xGF. They already beat Vancouver 7-2 on October 8. Minnesota, fourth on the site, brings the league's second-best power play (32.1%) into a building with the worst penalty kill in hockey, plus a defense that has held wingers far under their averages. Those two games are where Lankinen-versus-Merilainen matters most.

Detroit and Anaheim are the openings. Detroit's offense ranks 28th on a 7.8% shooting rate, its penalty kill is 28th, and it has allowed centers well above their norms, which suits Pettersson, Rossi and Karlsson. Anaheim, the road game to close the week, takes few shots (24.1 a game) but allows only 21.7, third-fewest, so expect a low-event game where Vancouver's thin shot volume gets even thinner. Splitting the soft half would be a decent week; anything more needs Merilainen at his best.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota power play vs. last-place PK
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota converts 32.1% of its power plays, second in the league, and Vancouver kills only 58.1%, last. Staying out of the box is the whole game plan. A couple of minors could decide it outright.

keyMatchups.title: Carolina's shot volume vs. Vancouver's
keyMatchups.body: Carolina is second in shots per game and holds a 60% CF %. Vancouver is last in shots and 29th in CF %. Unless the goalie steals it, the shot-share gap points to another lopsided night.

keyMatchups.title: Vancouver centers against Detroit
keyMatchups.body: Detroit has let centers outscore their expected points, ranking 26th at holding them down, and its penalty kill is 28th. This is the best spot of the week for Pettersson's line and the power play to produce. It's also the likeliest win.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal against Carolina and Minnesota: if Merilainen gets both, it signals the staff is reading the same split the numbers show.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the two halves of the luck to move in opposite directions. The 14.2% shooting will drift toward league average, and with the fewest shots in hockey that means scoring falls below its current 3.0 a game. The .865 team save percentage should rise, especially if Merilainen carries more of the starts, and a 58% penalty kill can't last at that level. Net, goals against should improve more than goals for declines, so this team ought to play better than its 41-point pace.

Better isn't good, though. A sub-40% expected-goals share is a bottom-two team's profile, and last year's 58 points came with a similar one. The realistic range is a finish near last season, somewhere in the mid-50s to mid-60s in points, with the year's real value in Buium's development, the young defense and the starter question.
swingFactors: Penalty kill rising toward league average
How far the shooting % falls on so few shots

confidence.note: Ten games is small, but the shot-share story matches last season's.
